source_refs.note: Chapter 11 exercise (PDF 259-260, printed 256-257), solved: five MCQs with keys worked out from the chapter (the book prints no MCQ key), ten short, five constructed response and three comprehensive questions with model answers, and eight numerical problems worked step by step; all eight printed answers agree.

blocks.prompt: 11.1 Relativistic mechanic yields results different from classical mechanics for objects moving with:

options.text: velocity equal to that of sound waves

blocks.explanation: Relativistic effects (time dilation, length contraction, mass variation) depend on √(1 − v²/c²). This factor is noticeably less than 1 only when v approaches c. At everyday speeds (even the speed of sound) it is almost 1, so classical and relativistic mechanics give the same results.

blocks.prompt: 11.2 If an observer is moving in the same direction as a sound wave, the velocity of the wave seems to be:
blocks.explanation: For sound, velocities are relative: the observer moving with the wave measures v_sound − v_observer, so the wave seems slower. (Light is different: by the second postulate its speed is c for every observer.)

blocks.prompt: 11.3 If the rest mass of a particle mₒ increases to m due to its high speed, then its kinetic energy is:
blocks.explanation: Total energy E = mc² and rest mass energy Eₒ = mₒc². The extra energy is due to motion, so K.E. = mc² − mₒc² = (m − mₒ)c² (Section 11.4).

blocks.prompt: 11.4 The speed of beam light of a car while moving with high speed as compared to its rest position is:
blocks.explanation: By the second postulate, the speed of light in free space is c for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer. So the car's light beam has the same speed c.

blocks.prompt: 11.5 A photon is a particle of light. What is its mass when it moves with 0.9 c?
blocks.explanation: A photon has zero rest mass (photons do not interact with the Higgs field, Section 12.7). 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg is the electron's mass and 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg the proton's. (In free space a photon always moves at c; a lower speed such as 0.9 c is possible only inside a medium.)

blocks.prompt: 11.1 What is meant by inertial frame of reference and a non-inertial frame of reference?
blocks.explanation:
Inertial frame: a frame in which the law of inertia holds; it is at rest or moves with uniform velocity (e.g. the Earth, a car moving with uniform velocity).
Non-inertial frame: an accelerated frame in which the law of inertia does not hold (e.g. a car that suddenly speeds up, stops or turns).

blocks.prompt: 11.2 What are the two postulates of special theory of relativity?
blocks.explanation:
1. The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames (principle of relativity).
2. The speed of light in free space has the same value c for all observers, regardless of the motion of the source or the observer (principle of constancy of light).

blocks.prompt: 11.3 Describe why it is impossible for a material particle to move with speed of light.
blocks.explanation:
By m = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²), as v → c the factor √(1 − v²/c²) → 0, so m → ∞.
An infinite mass needs an infinite force (infinite energy) to accelerate it. Since infinite force is not available, a material particle can never reach the speed of light.

blocks.prompt: 11.4 Does theory of relativity contradicts Newton's laws of motion? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation: No. Relativity extends Newton's mechanics. For speeds much smaller than c, v²/c² ≈ 0, so t = tₒ, ℓ = ℓₒ and m = mₒ, and the relativistic equations reduce to Newton's laws. Only near the speed of light do the results differ, and there relativity gives the correct (experimentally verified) results.

blocks.prompt: 11.5 What is meant by proper time, and proper length?
blocks.explanation:
Proper time (tₒ): the time interval between two events measured by an observer at rest in the frame in which the events occur.
Proper length (ℓₒ): the length of an object (or distance between two points) measured by an observer at rest relative to it.

blocks.prompt: 11.6 What is meant by relativistic mass, length and time?
blocks.explanation:
They are the mass, length and time measured for a body moving with speed v relative to the observer:
Mass: m = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²), greater than the rest mass.
Length: ℓ = ℓₒ√(1 − v²/c²), shorter than the proper length (along the motion only).
Time: t = tₒ/√(1 − v²/c²), longer than the proper time (time dilation).

blocks.prompt: 11.7 Why mass of a moving object increases?
blocks.explanation: According to special relativity, mass depends on speed: m = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²). As the speed increases, the energy given to the body increases its mass (E = mc²), i.e. its inertia increases. As v approaches c, a greater and greater force is needed to change its speed.

blocks.prompt: 11.8 All motion are relatives. Does space-time is absolute? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation: No. In relativity neither space nor time is absolute: lengths contract and time dilates, depending on the observer's frame. Space and time are joined into one four-dimensional continuum, space-time, which is itself curved near massive bodies. So space-time is not an absolute, fixed background.

blocks.prompt: 11.9 Explain that speed of light is an ultimate limit for any object.
blocks.explanation: As the speed of an object approaches c, its mass m = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²) tends to infinity, so the force or energy needed to accelerate it further tends to infinity. No object with mass can therefore reach, let alone exceed, the speed of light; c is the ultimate speed limit.

blocks.prompt: 11.10 Give examples where the results of special theory of relativity have been verified.
blocks.explanation:
1. Energy and mass changes in nuclear reactions agree exactly with E = mc² and Δm = ΔE/c².
2. Subatomic particles in accelerators: their mass increases with speed and they can never be pushed to c.
3. Pair production and annihilation (1.02 MeV for an electron-positron pair) confirm mass-energy equivalence.
4. Fast unstable particles (e.g. muons from cosmic rays) live longer than at rest: time dilation (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: 11.1 Speed of sound is affected by relative motion between the observer and the source. Does this apply to speed of light as well? Describe briefly.
blocks.explanation:
No. Sound is a mechanical wave in a medium, so its measured speed changes with the motion of the observer or source (v_sound ± v).
Light obeys the second postulate of special relativity: its speed in free space is the same, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer. For example, the light of a moving car's headlight is measured as c both by the driver and by a person standing on the road.

blocks.prompt: 11.2 Is it ever possible to see a star moving away from us at a uniform velocity equal to the velocity of light?
blocks.explanation: No. A star is a material body with rest mass. To move at the speed of light its mass m = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²) would become infinite, which would need infinite energy. So no star can move at the speed of light; it can only move at a speed less than c. (Whatever its speed, its light still reaches us with speed c.)

blocks.prompt: 11.3 If the speed of light is just 50 m s⁻¹, how would every day events appear to?
blocks.explanation:
Everyday speeds (cars, trains, aeroplanes) would then be close to c, so relativistic effects would be part of daily life:
1. Length contraction: moving vehicles would look shorter along their motion. A car at 30 m s⁻¹ has √(1 − 30²/50²) = 0.8, so a 5 m car would look 4 m long.
2. Time dilation: clocks of moving people would run slow; 1 h for the driver would be 1.25 h for us, and fast travellers would age more slowly.
3. Mass increase: moving bodies would become heavier and harder to accelerate; no vehicle could reach 50 m s⁻¹.
4. Simultaneity: events seen simultaneous by one observer would not be simultaneous for a moving observer.
5. We would see events late: light would take 2 s to cross 100 m.

blocks.prompt: 11.4 If the speed of light were infinite, what would the equations of special theory of relativity reduce to?
blocks.explanation:
If c → ∞, then v²/c² → 0 for every speed, so √(1 − v²/c²) → 1:
t = tₒ/√(1 − v²/c²) → t = tₒ (no time dilation)
ℓ = ℓₒ√(1 − v²/c²) → ℓ = ℓₒ (no length contraction)
m = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²) → m = mₒ (mass constant)
The equations reduce to those of classical (Newtonian) mechanics, in which time, length and mass are absolute.

blocks.prompt: 11.5 According to Einstein's equation; E = mc², is it possible to create a single electron from energy? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. Energy can change into mass, but charge must also be conserved. A photon has no charge, so energy cannot produce a single (negative) electron. It produces an electron together with its antiparticle, the positron (pair production): γ → e⁻ + e⁺. The photon's energy must be at least 2mₒc² = 1.02 MeV, and a nucleus must be nearby to conserve momentum (Chapter 12, Section 12.3).

blocks.prompt: 11.1 What is meant by the "frame of reference"? Distinguish between inertial frame of reference and non inertial frame of reference by giving examples.
blocks.explanation:
Frame of reference: any coordinate system relative to which measurements (position, motion) are taken. For example, the walls of a room for the position of a table, the laboratory for its experiments, a moving train for experiments done inside it, and the distant stars for the position of a spaceship. Rest and motion are relative: the walls of a moving train are at rest for its passengers but moving for a person on the ground.
Inertial and non-inertial frames differ as shown in the table. Strictly, the Earth is non-inertial (it rotates and revolves), but its acceleration is so small that it is treated as an inertial frame.

rows: The law of inertia (Newton's first law) holds in it
The law of inertia does not hold in it
At rest or moving with uniform velocity
Accelerated (speeding up, slowing down or turning)
A body at rest stays at rest unless an unbalanced force acts
A body at rest starts moving without any applied force (e.g. passengers jerk forward when a car brakes)
Special relativity deals with these frames
General relativity deals with these frames
Examples: the Earth (approximately), a car or train moving with uniform velocity
Examples: a car that suddenly stops or accelerates, a turning bus, a rotating merry-go-round

blocks.prompt: 11.2 Describe the Einstein's mass-energy equation; why cannot we observe its effects in everyday life? What are its significant consequences? Give examples.
blocks.explanation:
Mass-energy equation: mass and energy are interconvertible. The total energy E of a body of mass m is
E = mc²   (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
where m depends on speed. At rest, the rest mass energy is Eₒ = mₒc². The extra energy of a moving body is its kinetic energy: K.E. = mc² − mₒc² = (m − mₒ)c². A change of energy ΔE changes the mass by Δm = ΔE/c².
Why not seen in everyday life: c² = 9 × 10¹⁶ m² s⁻² is very large, so everyday energy changes give mass changes too small to measure. For example, heating 1 kg of water from 0 °C to 100 °C needs about 4.2 × 10⁵ J, which changes its mass by only Δm = 4.2 × 10⁵/9 × 10¹⁶ ≈ 4.7 × 10⁻¹² kg (beyond the chapter: uses the specific heat of water).
Significant consequences and examples:
1. A small mass holds a huge energy: 1 kg of mass is equivalent to 9 × 10¹⁶ J.
2. Nuclear reactions: the energy released in fission (nuclear power plants, atom bombs) and fusion (the Sun and stars) comes from a loss of mass, exactly as E = mc² predicts.
3. Energy can become matter: a photon of at least 1.02 MeV creates an electron-positron pair (pair production).
4. Matter can become energy: an electron and a positron annihilate into two gamma photons of 0.51 MeV each.
5. Rest mass energy of particles: e.g. the electron's rest mass energy is 0.51 MeV.

blocks.prompt: 11.3 State the Einstien's concept about the space-time. Describe the view of gravity according to this concept.
blocks.explanation:
Space-time concept:
1. Space is the three-dimensional extent in which all objects and events occur; time measures the sequence and duration of events and is treated as the fourth dimension.
2. In relativity time is not absolute; space and time are related, and they are unified into a single four-dimensional continuum called space-time, a mathematical model describing all points of space and time and their relations.
3. Space-time is curved, especially near massive bodies (and for speeds near c). It can be pictured as a stretched fabric sheet that sags when a heavy ball is placed on it; the more massive the body, the deeper the curve.
View of gravity:
1. Gravity is not treated as a force pulling bodies; it is the curvature of space-time produced by mass.
2. Bodies and light rays move along geodesics (the 'straight lines' of curved space-time). A body at rest or moving slowly near a massive object follows a geodesic towards it, which we see as gravitational attraction; a planet follows a geodesic around the Sun.
3. The theory explains why gravity follows the inverse square law (except in very strong fields), which Newton could not explain, and it gives Newton's results in ordinary fields, so it is an advancement over Newton's theory.
Evidence: the bending of starlight by the Sun measured during the 1919 solar eclipse (deflection 1.745 seconds of arc, as Einstein predicted) and the detection of gravitational waves (ripples of space-time) in 2015, announced in 2016.

blocks.prompt: 11.1 An electron is accelerated to a speed of 0.995 c which passes down an evacuated tube 500 m long. How long will the tube appear to the electron? (Ans: 50 m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: proper length of the tube ℓₒ = 500 m, v = 0.995 c
Required: length seen by the electron ℓ = ?
Formula: ℓ = ℓₒ √(1 − v²/c²)
ℓ = 500 m × √(1 − (0.995 c)²/c²)
ℓ = 500 m × √(1 − 0.990025)
ℓ = 500 m × √0.009975
ℓ = 500 m × 0.0999
ℓ = 49.9 m ≈ 50 m
Answer: the tube appears about 50 m long to the electron (same as the book's answer).

blocks.prompt: 11.2 A neutron, being not a stable particle, disintigerates in 20 minutes on the average. How long will it seem to exist if shoots out from a nucleus with a speed of 0.8 c? (Ans: 33.3 min)
blocks.explanation:
Given: proper time tₒ = 20 min, v = 0.8 c
Required: time measured by the observer t = ?
Formula: t = tₒ/√(1 − v²/c²)
t = 20 min/√(1 − (0.8 c)²/c²)
t = 20 min/√(1 − 0.64)
t = 20 min/√0.36
t = 20 min/0.6
t = 33.3 min
Answer: the neutron seems to exist for 33.3 min (same as the book's answer).

blocks.prompt: 11.3 A spaceship is measured 100 m long while it is at rest with respect to an observer, if this spaceship now flies by the observer with a speed of 0.99 c, what length will the observer find for the spaceship? (Ans: 14 m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: ℓₒ = 100 m, v = 0.99 c
Required: ℓ = ?
Formula: ℓ = ℓₒ √(1 − v²/c²)
ℓ = 100 m × √(1 − (0.99 c)²/c²)
ℓ = 100 m × √(1 − 0.9801)
ℓ = 100 m × √0.0199
ℓ = 100 m × 0.141
ℓ = 14.1 m ≈ 14 m
Answer: the observer finds the spaceship about 14 m long (same as the book's answer).

blocks.prompt: 11.4 The rest mass of an electron is 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Calculate the corresponding rest-mass energy. (Ans: 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J or 0.51 MeV)
blocks.explanation:
Given: mₒ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
Required: rest mass energy Eₒ = ?
Formula: Eₒ = mₒc²
Eₒ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg × (3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)²
Eₒ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 9 × 10¹⁶ J
Eₒ = 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J
In electron volts (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J):
Eₒ = 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ = 5.1 × 10⁵ eV
Eₒ = 0.51 MeV
Answer: Eₒ = 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J = 0.51 MeV (same as the book's answer).

blocks.prompt: 11.5 An electron is accelerated to a speed v = 0.85 c. Calculate its total energy and kinetic energy in electron volt. (Ans: 0.97 MeV, 0.459 MeV)
blocks.explanation:
Given: v = 0.85 c, rest mass energy of the electron Eₒ = mₒc² = 0.511 MeV (Problem 11.4: 0.51 MeV)
Required: total energy E = ?, kinetic energy K.E. = ?
Formulas: E = mc² = mₒc²/√(1 − v²/c²) and K.E. = E − mₒc²
√(1 − v²/c²) = √(1 − (0.85)²) = √(1 − 0.7225) = √0.2775 = 0.527
E = 0.511 MeV/0.527
E = 0.970 MeV ≈ 0.97 MeV
K.E. = E − mₒc² = 0.970 MeV − 0.511 MeV
K.E. = 0.459 MeV
Answer: total energy = 0.97 MeV (9.7 × 10⁵ eV); kinetic energy = 0.459 MeV (4.59 × 10⁵ eV), same as the book's answers.

blocks.prompt: 11.6 At what speed, would the mass of a proton in a particle accelerator be tripled? (Ans: 0.943 c)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 3mₒ
Required: v = ?
Formula: m = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²)
3mₒ = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²)
√(1 − v²/c²) = 1/3
1 − v²/c² = 1/9
v²/c² = 1 − 1/9 = 8/9 = 0.889
v = √0.889 c
v = 0.943 c (= 2.83 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
Answer: v = 0.943 c (same as the book's answer).

blocks.prompt: 11.7 The period of pendulum is measured to be 3 s in an inertial frame of reference. What will be the period measured by an observer in a spaceship with a constant speed of 0.95 c with respect to the pendulum? (Ans: 9.6 s)
blocks.explanation:
Given: proper time tₒ = 3 s, v = 0.95 c
Required: t = ?
Formula: t = tₒ/√(1 − v²/c²)
t = 3 s/√(1 − (0.95)²)
t = 3 s/√(1 − 0.9025)
t = 3 s/√0.0975
t = 3 s/0.312
t = 9.6 s
Answer: the observer measures a period of 9.6 s (same as the book's answer).

blocks.prompt: 11.8 Hypothetically, if a ball of mass 0.5 kg is projected with a velocity of 0.9 c, what will be its mass in flight? (Ans: 1.15 kg)
blocks.explanation:
Given: mₒ = 0.5 kg, v = 0.9 c
Required: m = ?
Formula: m = mₒ/√(1 − v²/c²)
m = 0.5 kg/√(1 − (0.9)²)
m = 0.5 kg/√(1 − 0.81)
m = 0.5 kg/√0.19
m = 0.5 kg/0.436
m = 1.15 kg
Answer: the mass in flight is 1.15 kg (same as the book's answer).
